title: Arrays, loops, and functions
goal: Store data in arrays, repeat work with while/until/for loops (over numbers, words, arguments, files, characters and lines), and organize scripts into functions that take arguments, set exit statuses and hand back results.

topics.title: Arrays
topics.examNote: Quiz 2 (2023) Q1C asked how to create an array holding 1, 2, 3 (`arr=(1 2 3)`) and Q1D how to get the number of elements (`${#arr[@]}`). Q4 (10 marks) started with `arr=("$@")` and needed `${arr[i]}`, element swaps, `${#arr[@]}` and `echo "${arr[@]}"`.

blocks.text:
An ordinary variable holds one value. An **array** is a single variable that holds many values. Each value is called an **element**, and each element has an **index**: a whole number that says where the element is stored.

Bash arrays are **zero-based**: 0 is the smallest legal index. But Bash is looser than Java or Python:

- you do not have to start filling the array at index 0, and
- the indexes do not have to be next to each other (an array with elements only at indexes 3 and 100 is fine).

An array with gaps in its indexes is called a **sparse** array.

Like other Bash variables, an array is created automatically the first time you assign to it.

### Creating an array

The most common way is to list the elements inside parentheses, separated by **spaces**:

blocks.code:
arr=(1 2 3)
echo "${arr[0]}"
echo "${arr[2]}"
blocks.caption: Create an array with three elements and print the elements at indexes 0 and 2 (Quiz 2 Q1C).

blocks.text:
Elements that contain spaces must be quoted, just like arguments to a command:

```bash
animals=("a dog" "a cat" "a fish")    # 3 elements
```

The notebook shows three more ways to create arrays:

```bash
arr[0]=hello                          # assign one element; creates arr if needed
declare -a y=(10 20 30)               # declare -a also creates an array
arr4=([100]=weird [0]=weirder [1]=weirdest)   # [index]=value sets specific indexes
```

To delete a whole array variable, use `unset arr`.

There are **no commas** between elements and **no spaces around `=`**. `arr=(1, 2, 3)` makes the elements `1,` `2,` and `3`. `arr = (1 2 3)` is a syntax error, because the shell reads `arr` as a command name.

blocks.caption: The comma becomes part of the element.

blocks.q: Show how to create a Bash array `arr` that contains the values 1, 2, and 3.
blocks.a: `arr=(1 2 3)`  (spaces between elements, no commas, no spaces around `=`)

blocks.text:
### Reading and changing one element

To get the element at index *i*, write `${arr[i]}`. The braces are **required**.

To change (or create) one element, write `arr[i]=value` (no `$`, no braces, because you are naming the variable, not expanding it).

The index is evaluated as an **arithmetic expression**, so you can use a variable or a calculation without a `$`: `${arr[i]}`, `${arr[i+1]}`, and `${arr[$i]}` all work.

blocks.code:
months=(Jan Feb Mar Apr)
i=2
echo "${months[i]}"
echo "${months[i+1]}"
months[0]=January
echo "${months[0]}"

Mar
Apr
January
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.text: Forgetting the braces is an easy mistake. `$arr` on its own expands to the element at index **0**. So `$arr[2]` expands `$arr` (the element at index 0) and then glues on the plain text `[2]`:

blocks.code:
arr=(red green blue)
echo $arr
echo $arr[2]
echo ${arr[2]}

red
red[2]
blue
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.q: `arr=(red green blue)`. What does `echo $arr[1]` print, and why?
blocks.a: `red[1]`. `$arr` means element 0 (`red`), and `[1]` is just text after it. Write `${arr[1]}` to get `green`.

blocks.text:
### Number of elements: `${#arr[@]}`

The number of elements in `arr` is written `${#arr[@]}` (or `${#arr[*]}`). Compare with `${#str}`, the length of a string, from Day 4: the `#` means "count".

blocks.code:
arr1=(hello)
arr2=(0 1 2 3 4)
arr3=([1]=goodbye)
arr4=([100]=weird [0]=weirder [1]=weirdest)
echo "# elems in arr1 : ${#arr1[@]}"
echo "# elems in arr2 : ${#arr2[@]}"
echo "# elems in arr3 : ${#arr3[@]}"
echo "# elems in arr4 : ${#arr4[@]}"
blocks.caption: From the arrays notebook. arr4 has 3 elements even though its largest index is 100.

blocks.code:
# elems in arr1 : 1
# elems in arr2 : 5
# elems in arr3 : 1
# elems in arr4 : 3
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.text: `${#arr}` (no `[@]`) is the length of the **string** in element 0, not the number of elements. With `arr=(apple kiwi)`, `${#arr}` is `5` but `${#arr[@]}` is `2`.

blocks.q: Given a Bash array `arr`, show how to get the number of elements in `arr`.
blocks.a: `${#arr[@]}` (or `${#arr[*]}`). This was Quiz 2 Q1D.

blocks.text:
### The indexes in use: `${!arr[@]}`

`${!arr[@]}` expands to the list of indexes that actually hold elements. This matters for sparse arrays, where the indexes are not simply 0, 1, 2, ...

blocks.caption: Indexes are listed in increasing order.

blocks.text: Looping over the indexes lets you print each index together with its element:

blocks.code:
months=(Jan Feb Mar Apr May)
for i in "${!months[@]}"; do
    elem=${months[i]}
    echo "months[$i] = $elem"
done

months[0] = Jan
months[1] = Feb
months[2] = Mar
months[3] = Apr
months[4] = May
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.q: `arr=([3]=c [7]=g)`. What do `${#arr[@]}` and `${!arr[@]}` expand to?
blocks.a: `${#arr[@]}` is `2` (two elements). `${!arr[@]}` is `3 7` (the indexes in use).

blocks.text:
### All the elements: `@` versus `*`, quoted versus unquoted

There are four ways to expand every element. They differ only when elements contain spaces:

| Expansion | What you get | Use it? |
|---|---|---|
| `${arr[@]}` | all elements, then **word splitting** | only if no element has spaces |
| `${arr[*]}` | same as above | only if no element has spaces |
| `"${arr[@]}"` | each element as **its own word**: `"${arr[0]}" "${arr[1]}" ...` | **almost always this one** |
| `"${arr[*]}"` | **one single word**: all elements joined by spaces | when you want one string |

Here are the four cases from the notebook. Watch how many times each loop body runs:

blocks.code:
animals=("a dog" "a cat" "a fish")
for i in ${animals[*]}; do echo $i; done
blocks.caption: Unquoted *: the elements are split into 6 words.

blocks.code:
a
dog
a
cat
a
fish
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.code:
animals=("a dog" "a cat" "a fish")
for i in ${animals[@]}; do echo $i; done
blocks.caption: Unquoted @: also 6 words.

blocks.code:
a
dog
a
cat
a
fish
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.code:
animals=("a dog" "a cat" "a fish")
for i in "${animals[@]}"; do echo $i; done
blocks.caption: Quoted @: one word per element (3 iterations). This is what you want.

blocks.code:
a dog
a cat
a fish
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.code:
animals=("a dog" "a cat" "a fish")
for i in "${animals[*]}"; do echo $i; done
blocks.caption: Quoted *: one single word (1 iteration).

blocks.code: a dog a cat a fish
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.q: Why is `"${arr[@]}"` almost always the right choice?
blocks.a: Quoting stops word splitting, so an element like `a dog` stays one word, and `@` (unlike `*`) keeps the elements as **separate** words. You get exactly one word per element, no more and no less. This is the same rule as `"$@"` for command line arguments.

blocks.text: To **print** the whole array on one line, `echo "${arr[@]}"` is the usual answer (echo prints its arguments separated by single spaces).

blocks.q: `animals=("a dog" "a cat")`. How many lines does `for x in "${animals[*]}"; do echo "$x"; done` print?
blocks.a: One line, `a dog a cat`. Quoted `*` joins all elements into a single word.

blocks.text:
### Appending and concatenating

`arr+=("$elem")` appends one element to the end of `arr`. `arr1+=("${arr2[@]}")` appends every element of `arr2` to `arr1`. The parentheses are essential.

blocks.code:
months=(Jan Feb Mar Apr)
months+=("May")
echo "${months[@]}"
echo "${#months[@]}"

Jan Feb Mar Apr May
5
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.text: New elements go **after the largest index in use**, not into the gaps:

blocks.caption: From the notebook: appending to a sparse array.

blocks.text: `arr+=x` without parentheses does **not** append an element. It appends the text `x` to the string in element 0:

blocks.code:
arr=(a b)
arr+=c
echo "${arr[@]}"
arr+=(d)
echo "${arr[@]}"

ac b
ac b d
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.q: Show how to append the value stored in `x` as a new element at the end of array `nums`.

blocks.text:
### Filling an array from arguments, the keyboard, or a file

**From the command line arguments.** `arr=("$@")` copies every argument into `arr`, one element per argument, keeping arguments with spaces whole. Quiz 2 Q4 started this way.

blocks.code:
$ cat args.sh
#!/bin/bash
arr=("$@")
echo "count: ${#arr[@]}"
echo "second: ${arr[1]}"
$ ./args.sh one "two three" four
count: 3
second: two three

blocks.text:
**From the keyboard.** `read -a arr` reads one line from standard input, splits it into words, and stores the words in `arr`. `read -p "Enter a list: " -a arr` prints a prompt first. Quotes typed by the user do **not** keep words together here.

**From a file.** `mapfile -t arr < file` (also called `readarray`) reads **every line** of standard input into `arr`, one line per element. The `-t` option removes the newline at the end of each line.

blocks.code:
mapfile -t students < students.txt
echo "${#students[@]} lines"
for elem in "${students[@]}"; do
    echo "$elem"
done
blocks.caption: students.txt is the notebook's file (a comment line plus 3 students).

blocks.code:
4 lines
# student number, last name, first name
12345,Parr,Jack-Jack
23456,Wazowski,Mike
98765,Best,Lucius
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.q: Which command reads each line of the file `data.txt` into its own element of the array `lines`, without the newlines?
blocks.a: `mapfile -t lines < data.txt` (`readarray -t lines < data.txt` is the same command).

blocks.text:
### Swapping two elements

Sorting algorithms (like the selection sort in Quiz 2 Q4) swap two elements. You need a temporary variable, as in Java:

### Key points

- Create: `arr=(1 2 3)`, `arr=("$@")`, `arr[i]=val`, `mapfile -t arr < file`. Spaces between elements, no commas.
- One element: `${arr[i]}` (braces required; `$arr` alone is element 0).
- Count: `${#arr[@]}`. Indexes in use: `${!arr[@]}`.
- All elements: `"${arr[@]}"` (one word per element). `"${arr[*]}"` is one single word.
- Append: `arr+=("$x")`. Arrays may be sparse; appends go after the largest index.

topics.title: Loops
topics.examNote: Quiz 2 (2023) Q1F: fill in `for arg in "$@"; do`. Quiz 2 Q4 used C-style loops over array indexes. Assignment 3 used `for f in *."$1"` with the no-match case (Q2), nested loops over `*/` and `"$@"` (Q3), and nested loops over the characters of a string (Q4).

blocks.text:
A **loop** runs the same commands again and again. Bash has four kinds:

1. `while` loops: repeat **while** a test command succeeds (exit status 0)
2. `until` loops: repeat **until** a test command succeeds (they run while it fails)
3. `for name in list` loops: run once for each word in a list
4. C-style `for (( ...; ...; ... ))` loops: counting with arithmetic

### `while` and `until`

Recall from Day 5 that `if` runs its body when the **test command** has exit status 0 ("true"). Loops use the same idea:

```bash
while test-command; do
    commands
done
```

The test command is usually `(( ))` for numbers or `[[ ]]` for strings and files. Both of these loops count down from 10 to 0:

blocks.code:
count=10
until (( count < 0 )); do
    echo $count
    count=$(( count - 1 ))
done | head -n 3
blocks.caption: until: keep going until count < 0 becomes true (output cut to 3 lines with head).

blocks.code:
count=3
while (( count > -1 )); do
    echo $count
    (( count-- ))
done
blocks.caption: while: keep going while count > -1 is true. (( count-- )) subtracts 1.

blocks.text:
Inside `(( ))` you can write variable names without `$`. `while true; do ... done` and `until false; do ... done` are infinite loops (you stop them with `break`, below).

The notebook's `collatz.sh` uses a `while` loop to print the Collatz sequence: halve *n* if it is even, otherwise replace it with 3*n*+1, until *n* is 1:

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash

# collatz.sh

if (( $# == 0 )); then
    echo "collatz.sh: missing positive integer argument" >&2
    exit 1
else
    val=$1
fi
if [[ ! $val =~ ^[-+]?[0-9]+$ ]]; then
    echo "collatz.sh: argument is not an integer" >&2
    exit 1
fi
if (( val < 1 )); then
    echo "collatz.sh: argument is not positive" >&2
    exit 2
fi
echo $val
while (( val != 1 )); do
    if (( val % 2 == 0 )); then
        val=$(( val / 2 ))
    else
        val=$(( 3 * val + 1 ))
    fi
    echo $val
done
blocks.caption: scripts/loops/collatz.sh

blocks.text: Forgetting to change the loop variable inside the body gives an **infinite loop**: the test never changes. Every `while`/`until` body must move toward the stopping condition (`(( count-- ))`, `shift`, reading the next line, ...).

blocks.q: What is the difference between `while` and `until`?
blocks.a: `while` repeats as long as the test command **succeeds** (exit status 0); `until` repeats as long as it **fails**, stopping as soon as it succeeds.

blocks.text:
### `for name in list`

```bash
for name in list; do
    commands
done
```

In Bash a **list** is just a sequence of words (strings separated by whitespace). The body runs once per word, with the variable *name* set to the current word. The list can come from many places:

blocks.code: for i in 3 2 1; do echo $i; done
blocks.caption: Words typed directly.

blocks.code:
str="this is   a string"
for s in $str; do
    echo $s
done
blocks.caption: An unquoted variable: word splitting breaks it into words (on purpose here).

blocks.code:
this
is
a
string
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.code: for i in {3..0}; do echo $i; done
blocks.caption: Brace expansion (Day 3).

blocks.code: for word in $(echo one two); do echo "[$word]"; done
blocks.caption: Command substitution. (The notebook warns: don't use $(seq ...) to count; use a C-style loop.)

blocks.code:
[one]
[two]
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.text: **Filename expansion (globs).** A glob in the list becomes the matching filenames, sorted. Each filename is one word, **even if it contains spaces**, because word splitting is not applied to glob results. Still quote `"$f"` inside the body, where word splitting *would* apply.

blocks.code:
for f in *.txt; do
    echo "file: $f"
done
blocks.caption: Directory contains a.txt, 'my notes.txt' and b.md.

blocks.code:
file: a.txt
file: my notes.txt
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.text: **The no-match case.** If a glob matches **nothing**, Bash leaves the pattern as plain text, so the loop runs **once** with the variable equal to the pattern itself:

blocks.code:
for f in *.pdf; do
    echo "file: $f"
done
blocks.caption: No .pdf files here, yet the body runs once.

blocks.code: file: *.pdf
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.text:
A script that then runs `mv "$f" ...` would fail with `mv: cannot stat '*.pdf'`. The standard fix (used in Assignment 3's `chext.sh`) is to skip anything that does not exist:

```bash
for f in *.pdf; do
    [[ -e $f ]] || continue     # no match: skip the literal *.pdf
    echo "file: $f"
done
```

(Another fix is to run `shopt -s nullglob` first, which makes a non-matching glob expand to nothing.)

**Directories only.** The glob `*/` matches only directories, and each name ends with `/`, e.g. `stu1/` and `stu 3/`. Assignment 3's `checksubs.sh` loops with `for d in */; do`.

blocks.q: A directory has no `.pdf` files. How many times does the body of `for f in *.pdf; do echo "$f"; done` run, and what does it print?
blocks.a: Once. It prints `*.pdf`, because a glob that matches nothing is left unchanged.

blocks.text:
### C-style `for`

```bash
for (( expr1; expr2; expr3 )); do
    commands
done
```

*expr1* runs once at the start (set up the counter). *expr2* is checked before each pass; the body runs while it is non-zero (true). *expr3* runs after each pass (update the counter). All three are arithmetic, so no `$` is needed on variables.

blocks.code:
for (( i=10; i >= 0; i -= 5 )); do
    echo $i
done

blocks.text: **Looping over the characters of a string.** Combine a C-style loop with `${#s}` (length) and `${s:i:1}` (the 1 character at offset *i*, Day 4). Assignment 3 Q4 (`hasdups`, `indexof`) is built on this pattern:

blocks.code:
s="cisc"
for (( i = 0; i < ${#s}; i++ )); do
    echo "$i: ${s:i:1}"
done

blocks.text: **Looping over an array by index** works the same way when the array is not sparse: `for (( i = 0; i < ${#arr[@]}; i++ )); do echo "${arr[i]}"; done`. To go backwards, start at `${#arr[@]} - 1` and use `i--`.

blocks.q: Write the header of a C-style loop that visits every index `i` of the string `s`.

blocks.text:
### Looping over the command line arguments: `"$@"`

`"$@"` expands to `"$1" "$2" "$3" ...`: one word per argument, spaces kept. So `for arg in "$@"` visits each argument exactly once (Quiz 2 Q1F asked for exactly this).

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash

# for_each_arg.sh

i=1
for arg in "$@"; do
    echo "\$${i} : $arg"
    (( i++ ))
done
blocks.caption: scripts/loops/for_each_arg.sh

blocks.code:
$ ./for_each_arg.sh arg1 "arg2 has some spaces" "arg3 has some spaces, too"
$1 : arg1
$2 : arg2 has some spaces
$3 : arg3 has some spaces, too

blocks.text: `bad_for_each_arg.sh` is identical except that it says `for arg in $@` (no quotes). Unquoted, `$@` becomes `$1 $2 $3`, and word splitting breaks every argument at its spaces:

blocks.code:
$ ./bad_for_each_arg.sh arg1 "arg2 has some spaces" "arg3 has some spaces, too"
$1 : arg1
$2 : arg2
$3 : has
$4 : some
$5 : spaces
$6 : arg3
$7 : has
$8 : some
$9 : spaces,
$10 : too

blocks.q: Why do the quotes in `"$@"` matter even though `$@` already means "all the arguments"?
blocks.a: Without quotes, the shell performs word splitting on the expanded arguments, so one argument with spaces turns into several words. With quotes, each argument is kept as exactly one word. That is why the bad script reports 10 arguments instead of 3.

blocks.text: **`shift`.** Another common pattern is a `while` loop with `shift`. `shift` moves every argument one place left (`$2` becomes `$1`, ...), drops the old `$1`, and lowers `$#` by one. `shift n` shifts by *n*.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash

# shift_arg.sh

while (( $# > 0 )); do
    # do something with first positional parameter
    # e.g., print its value
    echo "$1"

    # now shift positional parameters
    shift
done
blocks.caption: scripts/loops/shift_arg.sh

blocks.code:
$ ./shift_arg.sh arg1 "arg2 has some spaces"
arg1
arg2 has some spaces

blocks.q: Fill in the blank so the loop processes each command line argument: `for arg in ____; do`
blocks.a: `"$@"` (with the double quotes).

blocks.text:
### `break` and `continue`

- `break` leaves the loop immediately.
- `continue` skips the rest of this pass and starts the next one.

In nested loops, `break 2` / `continue 2` act on the loop one level further out.

blocks.code:
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do
    if (( i == 2 )); then
        continue
    fi
    if (( i == 5 )); then
        break
    fi
    echo $i
done

blocks.q: In the loop above, why is 6 never printed?
blocks.a: When `i` is 5, `break` ends the whole loop, so the pass for 6 never happens.

blocks.text:
### Reading a file one line at a time

```bash
while read -r line; do
    echo "$line"
done < "$file"
```

The redirection `< "$file"` after `done` feeds the file to the whole loop. Each time `read` runs, it reads the next line into `line`. `read` succeeds (status 0) while there is a line to read, and fails at the end of the file, which ends the loop. `-r` makes `read` treat backslashes as ordinary characters.

Skip comment lines with a regex test and `continue`:

blocks.code:
file="students.txt"
while read -r line; do
    if [[ $line =~ ^# ]]; then
        continue
    fi
    echo "$line"
done < "$file"

12345,Parr,Jack-Jack
23456,Wazowski,Mike
98765,Best,Lucius
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.text: `read` can also **split** each line into several variables using the characters in `IFS`. Writing `IFS=","` just before `read` sets it only for that command:

blocks.code:
while IFS="," read -r number last first; do
    if [[ $number =~ ^# ]]; then
        continue
    fi
    echo "$first $last"
done < students.txt

Jack-Jack Parr
Mike Wazowski
Lucius Best
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.text: The last line of a file is skipped by `while read` if it does **not** end with a newline (`read` fails on it). Also put the redirection after `done`. Writing `while read -r line < "$file"; do` re-opens the file on every pass, so it reads the first line forever.

blocks.q: Where does `< "$file"` go in a `while read` loop?
blocks.a: After `done`: `done < "$file"`. That way the whole loop reads from the file, one line per pass.

blocks.text:
### Nested loops

A loop inside a loop runs its whole inner loop once per pass of the outer loop. Assignment 3's `checksubs.sh` loops over directories (outer) and over the expected files (inner):

```bash
for d in */; do
    for f in "$@"; do
        if [[ ! -f $d$f ]]; then
            echo "$d" >&2
            break            # one message per directory is enough
        fi
    done
done
```

Note `$d$f`: `d` already ends with `/`, so `stu1/` + `README` is `stu1/README`.

blocks.q: In `checksubs.sh`, why is the path written `$d$f` and not `$d/$f`?
blocks.a: Names produced by the glob `*/` already end with `/` (e.g. `stu1/`), so `$d$f` gives `stu1/README`. (`$d/$f` gives `stu1//README`, which also works, because repeated slashes act like one.)

blocks.text:
### Key points

- `while`/`until` loop on a test command's exit status; use `(( ))` or `[[ ]]`.
- `for x in list`: lists come from words, unquoted variables, globs, `{a..b}`, `$( )`.
- A glob that matches nothing stays literal: guard with `[[ -e $f ]] || continue`.
- `for (( i = 0; i < n; i++ ))` for counting; `${s:i:1}` for the characters of a string.
- `for arg in "$@"` (quoted!) or `while (( $# > 0 )); do ...; shift; done` for arguments.
- `while read -r line; do ...; done < "$file"` reads a file line by line.

topics.title: Functions
topics.examNote: Quiz 2 (2023) Q4 (10 marks, a third of the quiz): write `sort` and `minidx` functions that sort an array; you choose how `minidx` returns its answer (global variable or `echo` + `$( )`). Assignment 3 Q4 wrote functions in a sourced file that print a result **and** set a return status (`hasdups`, `indexof`).

blocks.text:
A **function** is a named group of commands. Once defined, you run (call) it by typing its name, exactly like a command.

### Declaring a function

The course writes functions like this:

```bash
fname() {
    commands
}
```

Bash also accepts `function fname { commands }`. It is legal but less portable; you may see it on old tests (Quiz 2 Q4 used it), but write `fname() { ... }` yourself.

**Brace rules.** The `{` must be followed by a space or newline, and the `}` must start a new command: put it on its own line (course style), or after a `;` if you write the function on one line. Otherwise Bash cannot tell that the brace is a delimiter and you get a syntax error:

blocks.code:
$ cat bad.sh
#!/bin/bash
fname() {echo "inside function"
}
$ ./bad.sh
./bad.sh: line 2: syntax error near unexpected token `{echo'
./bad.sh: line 2: `fname() {echo "inside function"'
blocks.caption: No space after {.
The } is on the same line as echo, so Bash treats it as one more argument to echo and the function body never ends.

blocks.code:
greet() { echo "Hello"; }
greet
blocks.caption: One-line form: note the space after { and the ; before }.

blocks.code: Hello
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.text: A function must be **defined before the line that calls it runs**. Bash reads a script top to bottom; calling a function earlier gives `command not found`. That is why scripts put their functions at the top.

blocks.q: Why is `say() {echo hi; }` a syntax error?
blocks.a: There is no space or newline after `{`, so Bash reads `{echo` as one word instead of seeing the brace that opens the body.

blocks.text:
### Arguments: `$1`, `$#`, `$@` inside a function

Function parameters have **no names**. While a function runs, the positional parameters `$1`, `$2`, ..., `$#` and `$@` are **temporarily replaced** by the function's own arguments. When the function returns, the script's arguments are back. Calling a function with the wrong number of arguments is not an error (missing ones are just empty), exactly like a script.

blocks.code:
$ cat params.sh

blocks.text: Inside a function you **cannot see the script's `$1`**. If the function needs the script's arguments, pass them in: `fname "$@"` (quoted, so arguments with spaces stay whole).

blocks.q: Inside a function, what does `$1` mean?
blocks.a: The first argument passed **to the function** (not the script's first argument). `$#` is the number of arguments passed to the function.

blocks.text:
### Exit status and `return`

A function sets an **exit status**, just like a command:

- by default, the exit status of the **last command** it ran, or
- explicitly with `return n`, which stops the function immediately.

The status is always 0-255: `return n` keeps only the lowest 8 bits of *n* (so `return 256` gives 0 and `return 300` gives 44). Read it with `$?` right after the call, or use the call directly as the test of an `if` or `while`:

blocks.code:
is_int() {
    if [[ $1 =~ ^[-+]?[0-9]+$ ]]; then
        return 0
    else
        return 1
    fi
}
is_int 42; echo "42 -> $?"
is_int 4x; echo "4x -> $?"
if is_int -7; then echo "-7 is an int"; fi
blocks.caption: is_int is from max.sh. 0 means true (success).

blocks.code:
42 -> 0
4x -> 1
-7 is an int
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.code:
f() { return 300; }
f; echo $?
blocks.caption: 300 does not fit in 8 bits: 300 - 256 = 44.

blocks.text: `return` is **not** a way to hand back a result like 1000 or a string. Use it only for success/failure. Also don't confuse `return` with `exit`: `exit` inside a function ends the **whole script**.

blocks.code:
$ cat quit.sh
#!/bin/bash
stop() {
    exit 3
}
echo before
stop
echo after
$ ./quit.sh; echo "status $?"
before
status 3
blocks.caption: 'after' never prints.

blocks.q: A function's last command is `return 257`. What is `$?` after the call?
blocks.a: `1` (257 - 256). Only the lowest 8 bits are kept.

blocks.text:
### Getting a value out of a function

There are two techniques.

**1. Print it, and capture it with command substitution.** The function `echo`es the result; the caller writes `var=$(fname args)`. This is how `max.sh` works:

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash

# max.sh

# prints the maximum of two integer arguments
# prints the first integer if both values are equal
max2() {
    if (( $1 >= $2 )); then
        echo $1
    else
        echo $2
    fi
}

# exits with 0 if argument is an integer, 1 otherwise
is_int() {
    if [[ $1 =~ ^[-+]?[0-9]+$ ]]; then 
        return 0
    else
        return 1
    fi
}


if (( $# == 0 )); then 
    exit 1
fi
if is_int "$1"; then 
    hi=$1
else 
    exit 2
fi
while (( $# > 0 )); do
    if is_int "$1"; then 
        hi=$(max2 $hi $1)
    else
        exit 2
    fi
    shift
done
echo $hi
blocks.caption: scripts/functions/max.sh

blocks.code:
$ ./max.sh 1 5 7 4
7
$ ./max.sh; echo $?
1
$ ./max.sh 3 x; echo $?
2

blocks.text:
The downside: `$( )` runs the function in a **subshell** (a copy of the shell), which is slow, and any variables the function sets are lost when the subshell ends.

**2. Set a variable the caller can see.** Because of dynamic scoping (next section), a function can assign to an ordinary (non-local) variable and the caller reads it afterwards. `remax.sh` is `max.sh` rewritten so that `max2` stores its answer in `hi`:

```bash
max2() {
    if (( $1 >= $2 )); then
        hi=$1
    else
        hi=$2
    fi
}
...
        max2 $hi $1        # instead of hi=$(max2 $hi $1)
```

blocks.code:
$ ./remax.sh 5 10 1
10

blocks.text: Quiz 2 Q4's `minidx` used this second technique: it set a global variable `idx` that `sort` then used.

blocks.q: Why can't you get a result out of a function with `x=$(f)` if `f` returns its answer by setting a global variable?
blocks.a: `$( )` runs `f` in a subshell. The variable is set in that copy of the shell and disappears when the subshell ends; also `$( )` captures only what `f` **prints**. Pick one technique: print + `$( )`, or set a variable + call `f` normally.

blocks.q: Function `double` prints twice its argument. Store `double 21`'s result in `x`.
blocks.a: `x=$(double 21)`

blocks.text:
### Dynamic scoping

Bash uses **dynamic scoping**: the variables a function can see depend on **who called it**, not on where it is written. By default every variable is global: a function sees the caller's variables, and anything it assigns stays visible to the caller after it returns.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash

# dynamic_scope.sh

f() {
    echo "  a at beginning of f()   = $a"
    a="f: hello"
    g
    echo "  a at end of f()         = $a"
    echo "  b at end of f()         = $b"
}

g() {
    echo "    a at beginning of g() = $a"
    b="g: goodbye"
    echo "    a at end of g()       = $a"
}

a="hello"
echo "a before calling f()      = $a"
f
echo "a after calling f()       = $a"
echo "b after calling f()       = $b"
blocks.caption: scripts/functions/dynamic_scope.sh

blocks.code:
$ ./dynamic_scope.sh
a before calling f()      = hello
  a at beginning of f()   = hello
    a at beginning of g() = f: hello
    a at end of g()       = f: hello
  a at end of f()         = f: hello
  b at end of f()         = g: goodbye
a after calling f()       = f: hello
b after calling f()       = g: goodbye

blocks.text:
Trace: the script sets `a`; `f` sees it and changes it; `g` (called by `f`) sees the changed `a` and **creates** `b`; `b` is then visible in `f` and in the main script.

### `local` variables

This sharing can cause bugs. Here a function accidentally changes the loop counter `i`:

blocks.code:
some_function() {
    i=100
}
for (( i = 0; i < 10; i++ )); do
    echo $i
    some_function
done
blocks.caption: Only one pass: some_function sets i to 100, then i++ makes 101, and 101 < 10 is false.

blocks.text: `local i=100` creates a **new** `i` that exists only while `some_function` runs, so the script's `i` is untouched:

blocks.code:
some_function() {
    local i=100
}
for (( i = 0; i < 3; i++ )); do
    echo $i
    some_function
done

blocks.text: A `local` variable is still visible to any function that the declaring function **calls** (dynamic scoping again):

blocks.code:
0
some_other_function i = 100
1
some_other_function i = 100
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.text: Good habit: declare every helper variable in a function `local` (`local i j`, `local s=$1`) unless you deliberately use it to return a value.

blocks.q: What does `local` do?
blocks.a: It creates a variable that belongs to the current function call (and is visible to functions it calls) and disappears when the function returns, so it cannot overwrite a variable of the same name in the caller.

blocks.text:
### A file of functions and `source`

A file can hold only function definitions (Assignment 3's `Q4.sh` had no shebang). `source ./funcs.sh` (or `. ./funcs.sh`) runs that file **in the current shell**, so its functions become defined there and you can call them, or use them from another script:

blocks.code:
$ cat funcs.sh
# funcs.sh -- source me
shout() {
    echo "$1!"
    return 5
}
$ source ./funcs.sh
$ shout hello there
hello!
$ echo $?
5

blocks.text: Running `./funcs.sh` instead would define the functions in a **separate** process that ends immediately, so nothing would be defined in your shell.

blocks.q: Why must a file of functions be loaded with `source ./funcs.sh` rather than run with `./funcs.sh`?
blocks.a: `source` runs the file in the **current** shell, so the functions stay defined there. `./funcs.sh` runs in a separate process; the definitions vanish when it ends.

blocks.text:
### Key points

- Define with `name() { ... }` before calling; space after `{`, `}` on its own line (or after `;`).
- Call like a command: `name arg1 "arg 2"`. Inside, `$1`, `$#`, `$@` are the function's arguments; pass the script's with `name "$@"`.
- `return n` sets the exit status (0-255, 0 = success); `exit` ends the whole script.
- Results: `echo` it and capture with `var=$(name ...)`, or assign a global variable.
- Variables are global and dynamically scoped; use `local` for helpers.
- `source ./file.sh` loads a file of functions into the current shell.

quiz.q: Which line creates an array `arr` holding the three values 1, 2 and 3?
quiz.explain: Elements go in parentheses separated by spaces. Commas would become part of the elements (`1,`), square brackets do not make an array, and spaces around `=` make Bash run `arr` as a command.

quiz.q: What does this print?
quiz.explain: `${#arr[@]}` is the number of elements (3). Indexes start at 0, so index 1 is the second element, 20.

quiz.q: What does this print?
quiz.code:
arr=(red green blue)
echo $arr
echo $arr[2]
quiz.explain: `$arr` alone means element 0. In `$arr[2]` only `$arr` is expanded; `[2]` is plain text. You need `${arr[2]}` to get `blue`.

quiz.q: What does this print?
quiz.code:
arr=([3]=c [7]=g)
arr+=(h)
echo "${!arr[@]}"
echo "${#arr[@]}"
quiz.explain: The array is sparse: indexes 3 and 7. Appending puts `h` after the largest index, at 8. There are 3 elements, even though the largest index is 8.

quiz.q: What does this print?
quiz.code:
pets=("a dog" "a cat")
for x in "${pets[@]}"; do echo "<$x>"; done
for x in "${pets[*]}"; do echo "<$x>"; done
for x in ${pets[@]}; do echo "<$x>"; done
quiz.explain: Quoted `@`: one word per element (2 passes). Quoted `*`: one single word (1 pass). Unquoted: word splitting gives 4 words (4 passes).

quiz.q: Array `files` holds filenames, some containing spaces. Which loop visits each filename exactly once?
quiz.explain: `"${files[@]}"` expands to one quoted word per element. Unquoted `@` splits names at spaces; quoted `*` gives one big word; `"$files"` is only element 0.

quiz.q: What does this print?
quiz.code:
arr=(a b)
arr+=c
arr+=(d)
echo "${arr[@]}"
echo "${#arr[@]}"
quiz.explain: `arr+=c` without parentheses appends the text `c` to element 0, making `ac`. `arr+=(d)` adds a new element. So 3 elements: `ac`, `b`, `d`.

quiz.q: The script `count.sh` is run as `./count.sh one "two three" four`. What does it print?
quiz.code:
#!/bin/bash
arr=("$@")
echo "${#arr[@]}"
echo "${arr[1]}"
echo "${arr[2]}"
quiz.explain: `arr=("$@")` makes one element per argument, keeping `two three` whole. So there are 3 elements; index 1 is `two three` and index 2 is `four`.

quiz.q: The file `colors.txt` contains three lines: `red`, `light green`, `blue`. What does this print?
quiz.code:
mapfile -t c < colors.txt
echo "${#c[@]}"
echo "${c[1]}"
quiz.explain: `mapfile -t` stores one line per element (spaces inside a line are kept) and strips the newlines. 3 lines give 3 elements; index 1 is the second line.

quiz.q: Write the Bash lines that swap the elements at indexes `i` and `j` of the array `arr`.
quiz.explain: You need a temporary variable, otherwise the first assignment overwrites a value you still need. `${arr[$i]}` is equally fine.

while (( count > 0 )); do

    (( count-- ))
done
echo done
quiz.explain: The body runs while `count > 0`: for 3, 2 and 1. When count reaches 0 the test fails and the loop ends.

until (( n > 20 )); do

for arg in $@; do (( n++ )); done

done

quiz.q: In `chext.sh`, why does the loop `for f in *."$1"; do` start its body with `[[ -e $f ]] || continue`?
options: Because when no file matches, `f` is the literal pattern, which does not exist
To skip files with spaces in their names
To make the loop run in sorted order
quiz.explain: A glob with no match is left unchanged, so the body would run once with `f` equal to e.g. `*.txt`, and `mv` would fail. `-e` tests whether the name exists; if not, `continue` skips it. It has nothing to do with directories, spaces or sorting.

while (( $# > 0 )); do
    echo "$#: $1"
    shift
done
quiz.explain: Each `shift` removes the first argument and lowers `$#` by 1. The loop stops when `$#` reaches 0.

quiz.q: What does this print?

    if (( i % 2 == 0 )); then
        continue
    fi
    if (( i > 4 )); then

`function f {` then `echo hi` and `}` on separate lines

in f: Y
in script: X

quiz.q: What does this print?
quiz.explain: An exit status is only 8 bits (0-255). 300 - 256 = 44.

quiz.q: What does this print?
quiz.explain: The function prints its result; `$( )` captures that output into `x`.

quiz.q: What does this print?
quiz.answer:
g sees inner
f has changed
main has outer

quiz.q: What does this print?
quiz.code:
f() {
    i=100
}
for (( i = 0; i < 3; i++ )); do
    echo $i
    f
done
echo "after: $i"
quiz.explain: `f` has no `local`, so it changes the loop's `i` to 100. Then `i++` makes it 101, `101 < 3` is false, and the loop ends after one pass.

quiz.q: A function `check` runs `exit 1` when it finds a problem. What happens when a script calls `check` and the problem is found?
options: The whole script stops with exit status 1
Nothing: `exit` is not allowed in a function
quiz.explain: `exit` always ends the whole script (the current shell). To stop only the function and set its status, use `return 1`.

quiz.q: Inside a script, show how to call the function `process` so that it receives all of the script's command line arguments.
quiz.explain: Inside `process`, `$1`, `$2`, ... are then the script's arguments. Quote `$@` so arguments with spaces stay whole.

*(Quiz 2, 2023, Q4, 10 marks.)* The **selection sort** algorithm sorts an array `arr` of `n` integers:

```
for j = 0, 1, 2, ..., n-1
    idx = minidx(j)
    swap arr[j] and arr[idx]
```

`minidx(j)` finds the index of the minimum element of `arr` from index `j` to the end. For `arr` = `[0, 3, 1, 4, 2]`: `minidx(0)` is 0, `minidx(1)` is 2, `minidx(2)` is 2, `minidx(3)` is 4, `minidx(4)` is 4.

Complete the script so that it sorts its command line arguments (always integers) with selection sort, using functions `sort` and `minidx`, and prints the sorted elements on a single line. The script already contains:

```bash
arr=("$@")
sort
```

You choose how to call `minidx` and how it returns its value. No error checking is required. (The quiz wrote `function sort {`; `sort() {` is the course style and equally correct.)
write.solution:
#!/bin/bash

# minidx START
# sets the global variable idx to the index of the smallest
# element of arr from index START to the end of arr
minidx() {
    local i
    idx=$1
    for (( i = $1 + 1; i < n; i++ )); do
        if (( arr[i] < arr[idx] )); then
            idx=$i
        fi
    done
}

# sort: selection sort of the global array arr
sort() {
    local j tmp
    n=${#arr[@]}
    for (( j = 0; j < n; j++ )); do
        minidx "$j"
        tmp=${arr[j]}
        arr[j]=${arr[idx]}
        arr[idx]=$tmp
    done
}

# places the command line arguments into arr and calls sort
arr=("$@")
sort

# print the sorted elements of arr on a single line
echo "${arr[@]}"
write.explain:
**Plan.** Two functions share the global array `arr` (dynamic scoping: every function sees the script's variables).

**`sort`.** First compute `n=${#arr[@]}`, the number of elements; `minidx` will see `n` too because it is not `local`. The C-style loop runs `j` from 0 to n-1. Each pass calls `minidx "$j"` and then swaps `arr[j]` with `arr[idx]` using a temporary variable `tmp`. Without `tmp`, the first assignment would destroy a value we still need.

**`minidx`.** Its argument `$1` is the start index. It assumes the smallest is at the start (`idx=$1`), then the loop checks every later index `i`; when `arr[i]` is smaller than the current best `arr[idx]`, it remembers `i`. Inside `(( ))` array elements can be written `arr[i]` without `$` or braces.

**Returning the index.** `return` cannot be used: it only gives an exit status (0-255, and 0 means success). Instead `minidx` sets the **global variable `idx`**, like `max2` in `remax.sh`. The other correct way: `minidx` ends with `echo "$idx"` and `sort` writes `idx=$(minidx "$j")`.

**`local`.** `i`, `j` and `tmp` are local so the two loops cannot overwrite each other's counters (the `some_function` bug from the notebook). If both functions used a global `i`, `minidx` would change `sort`'s loop variable.

**Printing.** `echo "${arr[@]}"` prints all elements separated by single spaces on one line.

Trace for `./sort.sh 0 3 1 4 2`: j=0 leaves 0 in place; j=1 swaps 3 with the 1 at index 2; j=2 swaps 3 with the 2 at index 4; j=3 and j=4 change nothing. Output `0 1 2 3 4`.

rubric.item: `n` is set to `${#arr[@]}` before it is used
`sort` loops `j` from 0 to n-1 (C-style `for (( ))` or equivalent)
`sort` calls `minidx` with `j` and obtains the index (global variable or `$( )`)
Correct swap of `arr[j]` and `arr[idx]` using a temporary variable
`minidx` starts at its argument and loops to the end comparing `arr[i]` with the current minimum
`minidx` makes the minimum index available to the caller (sets a global or echoes it; not `return`)
Prints the sorted array on one line with `echo "${arr[@]}"`

pitfalls: Using `return $idx` to hand back the index: it is an exit status, limited to 0-255, and a non-zero status means failure.
Using the same global loop variable `i` in both functions, so `minidx` breaks `sort`'s loop. Declare loop variables `local`.
Writing `$arr[i]` instead of `${arr[i]}` outside `(( ))`.
Swapping without a temporary variable (`arr[j]=${arr[idx]}; arr[idx]=${arr[j]}` copies the same value twice).

# funcs.sh -- a file of functions; use it with:  source ./funcs.sh

# hasdups STR
# prints "c:i = c:j" for the first character of STR that is repeated
# (i is its first index, j the index of its next copy) and returns 0;
# prints nothing and returns 1 if STR has no repeated characters
hasdups() {
    local s=$1
    local n=${#s}
    local i j
    for (( i = 0; i < n; i++ )); do
        for (( j = i + 1; j < n; j++ )); do
            if [[ ${s:i:1} == "${s:j:1}" ]]; then
                echo "${s:i:1}:$i = ${s:j:1}:$j"
                return 0
            fi
        done
    done
    return 1
}

# indexof CH STR
# prints the index of the first CH in STR and returns 0;
# prints -1 and returns 1 if CH is not in STR
indexof() {
    local ch=$1
    local str=$2
    local i
    for (( i = 0; i < ${#str}; i++ )); do
        if [[ ${str:i:1} == "$ch" ]]; then
            echo "$i"
            return 0
        fi
    done
    echo -1
    return 1
}

The right-hand side of `==` inside `[[ ]]` is **quoted**: unquoted, it is a glob pattern, so a `*` character in the string would match anything. Quoted, it is compared literally.

#!/bin/bash

# checksubs.sh FILE...
# prints (to stderr) the name of each subdirectory of the cwd that is missing
# one of the FILEs as a regular file; exit status 1 if any were missing, else 0

status=0
for d in */; do
    [[ -d $d ]] || continue          # no subdirectories: */ did not match
    for f in "$@"; do
        if [[ ! -f $d$f ]]; then
            echo "$d" >&2

    done
done
